paragraphs: The following assessments concern machining and tool and die making work performed by machinists and tool and die makers. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

The core work of machinists and tool and die makers is to turn metal into conforming precision parts, instruments, tools, and dies according to drawings and specifications: interpret part drawings and specifications and sequence operations, calculate dimensions and tolerances, select metals and alloys, set up and operate lathes, milling machines, grinding machines, drilling machines, and CNC equipment, write or call CNC programs, assemble and finish tools, dies, fixtures, and gauges, inspect with measuring tools and gauge blocks, conduct trial runs and adjustments, maintain equipment, and record results.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional part drawing and tolerance requirements, including 1 process routing sheet and 1 first article inspection record. Within 60 minutes, write out the choice of machining method, operation sequence, measuring tool selection, first article inspection, and nonconformance handling steps. Do not use real company, drawing, or customer data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether you first understood the drawing and tolerances, arranged operations reasonably around datums, specified measuring tools and inspection methods, and provided correction and escalation paths for nonconformances. Then ask whether you can remain focused and rigorous under high precision requirements and time pressure, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for machining accuracy and inspection records.

On this page, machinists and tool and die makers refers to the combined BLS OOH category, covering O*NET 51-4041.00 Machinists and 51-4111.00 Tool and Die Makers: workers who set up and operate equipment to produce precision metal parts, instruments, tools, and dies. Machinists mainly machine precision parts; tool and die makers additionally analyze specifications and assemble and repair dies, cutting tools, jigs, fixtures, gauges, and hand tools. Work includes calculating dimensions and tolerances, machining and assembling parts, measuring and inspecting, setting up and operating machine tools including CNC equipment, reading drawings, selecting metals, assembling and finishing, and conducting trial runs and adjustments. Work mainly takes place in machine shops and factories. This page excludes adjacent roles such as CNC programmers, industrial machinery mechanics, and mechanical assemblers.

entries: Inputs: metals and alloys, part drawings / blueprints and specifications, dimensional and tolerance requirements, machine tools such as lathes, milling machines, grinding machines, and drilling machines, CNC systems, fixtures and cutting tools, measuring tools and gauge blocks, assembly and finishing supplies, process routes, and inspection records.

Inspectable outputs: parts machined to tolerance, assembled and finished tools and dies, fixtures and gauges, CNC programs, first article and in-process inspection records, trial run and adjustment records, machine tool maintenance records, and nonconformance handling records.

Complete workflow: study drawings and specifications and sequence operations → select metals → clamp and align the workpiece and set up the machine and tools → perform trial cuts and first article inspection → machine / assemble and monitor → measure, inspect, and conduct trial runs → finish, adjust, and record results.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether machining methods, operation sequences, material choices, and tool choices are appropriate; how to choose datums and clamping arrangements; how to meet tolerances and surface requirements; when first article and in-process inspection indicate nonconformance; and whether deviations call for parameter adjustments, rework, or scrapping.

Environment and pace: mainly machine shops and factories, with most workers employed full time during regular hours; overtime, night shifts, and weekends are common. Accuracy is extremely important, equipment speed influences work pace, and workers face time pressure, hazardous equipment, and noise exposure.

Research inputs: occupational identities, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest codes, education, and Job Zones for O*NET 51-4041.00 and 51-4111.00. The combined BLS OOH category supplies pay, employment, and outlook data. These findings do not establish qualifications, pay, or employment categories for mainland China.

Check first: part drawings and specifications, machining and assembly operations, clamping and datums, measuring tools and inspection methods, metals and heat treatment, machine and tool condition, safety protection requirements, and requirements for handling and documenting nonconformances.

Work cycle: begin with drawing review and operation sequencing, continue through material selection, clamping and alignment, machine setup, trial cuts and first article inspection, machining / assembly and monitoring, and finish with measurement, inspection, trial runs, adjustments, maintenance records, and corrections. Do not begin batch machining before all first article and safety conditions are confirmed.

Boundaries with adjacent duties: this page covers the combined functions of machinists and tool and die makers. CNC programmers handle programming and process documentation, industrial machinery mechanics handle equipment installation and repair, and mechanical assemblers assemble components. Their process authorization and final quality responsibilities cannot be treated as interchangeable with those on this page.

Tool and die makers analyze specifications and assemble and repair dies, fixtures, measuring tools, and hand tools. The machinist portion focuses more on machining and inspecting general precision parts; tool and die making is the other part of the combined category.

CNC programmers write and optimize CNC programs and process documents. Machinists and tool and die makers set up and operate machine tools, clamp and align workpieces, and conduct precision inspection. The roles often collaborate but have different authorizations and outputs.

Lathe operators machine rotational parts on lathes, while grinding machine operators handle grinding and finishing. Machinists and tool and die makers cover setup and operation across multiple machine tools and take responsibility for overall machining accuracy and inspection.

Industrial machinery mechanics install, diagnose, and repair industrial machinery and equipment. Machinists and tool and die makers focus on machining and tool and die production; equipment repair belongs to a different area of responsibility.
Boundaries of AI impact on machinists and tool and die makers

Candidate editorial experiment: organize process instructions using fictional dimensions, assembly records, and inspection records. CAD, CAM, and CNC automation do not establish generative AI adoption. Authorized personnel must review programs, clamping, first articles, die trials, and quality dispositions against the target process.

Occupational sources describe the tasks and objects actually handled in this occupation: drawings and tolerances, machines and tools, fixtures and measuring tools, metals, CNC programs, and inspection records. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; pay or employment data do not substitute for AI evidence.

The editorial task breakdown proposes only candidates for validation. This round obtained no ranking of automation difficulty by stage or evidence of generative AI adoption outcomes. BLS discussions of mechanical automation do not establish AI replacement.

Human control points include confirming drawings and processes, checking datums and measuring tools, judging first article and in-process inspection results, completing assembly, finishing, and trial runs, and taking responsibility for machining accuracy and inspection records.

Start with an offline process exercise using entirely fictional part drawings and tolerance requirements. Record operation sequences, clamping, measuring tools, and inspection boundaries, without relying on unverified automated programs to replace first article confirmation.
Editorial suggestion: tools may assist programming, path optimization, design, and inspection data summaries. Current materials do not establish widespread adoption of these systems by manufacturers.
Follow drawing, process, and safety requirements, retaining human judgment and records.

This round did not establish a match between the combined BLS occupations and a separately reported Chinese wage category. The NBS2025 manufacturing figures of 113594/76055 and national nonprivate figure of 129441 yuan are enterprise industry proxies, not medians or starting pay for the combined category or either suboccupation, nor evidence of their industry distribution in China.

Scope note: National Bureau of Statistics figures for 2025 average annual wages in manufacturing are {{fact:cn-mfg-nonprivate-wage}} for urban nonprivate units and {{fact:cn-mfg-private-wage}} for urban private units. The total for urban nonprivate units nationwide is {{fact:cn-national-nonprivate-wage}}. All are industry figures and do not represent this occupation's median or starting pay.

Category boundary: enterprise remuneration survey information from the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is published by occupation / position and may be used to look up pay for related machining jobs. This page has not obtained an entry that precisely matches the combined BLS OOH category, so it is not used as a national occupational median. Refer to releases by the responsible authority.

Insufficient evidence: a national occupational wage median, reference period, and matching scope for machinists and tool and die makers in mainland China were not obtained. This page displays only industry proxies explicitly labeled as such, and does not fill the gap with proxy figures or US figures.
US pay and employment scope for machinists and tool and die makers: the combined BLS OOH category

The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook reports median annual pay of $59,620, about $28.66 per hour, for this combined category in 2025. Employment was about 344,900 in 2025 and is projected to decline by about 1% during 2025–2035, a change of about -2,200, with about 30,400 openings per year, all arising from replacement needs. Separate occupational medians are $58,750 for machinists and $64,050 for tool and die makers (May 2025). These are US national figures; combined and separate occupational figures must not be mixed.

Pay statistics: the figures above cover the US nationally. The combined median and separate occupational medians are listed separately. A median does not represent starting pay or an individual's take-home income.

How to interpret these positions: a median is not a beginner or senior grade and cannot be interchanged with a separate occupational median. Employment size, the projected percentage decline, and average annual openings are occupational statistics and must be explained separately from individual opportunities.

BLS lists employers separately for 2025: fabricated metal products 35%, machinery 21%, and transportation equipment 13% for machinists; transportation equipment 25%, machinery 23%, and fabricated metal products 20% for tool and die makers. These are not employment shares for the combined category. Pay and industries must be checked separately for each suboccupation.

Employment size and scope reminder: the combined category had about 344,900 jobs in 2025 and is projected to decline by about 1% during 2025–2035. Citations must state the year, coverage, and combined scope; separate occupational medians and combined figures cannot be spliced across scopes.
Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can understand drawings and patiently handle dimensional tolerances, stand and operate equipment attentively for long periods, measure and inspect to specifications and keep truthful records, complete assembly and finishing, and take responsibility for accuracy and safety. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses and cannot replace experience with real tasks.
Positive signals: understanding drawings and tolerances, sequencing operations around datums and processes, patiently measuring and checking, and following safety and equipment procedures.

Reasons for caution: reluctance to check tolerances and datums, difficulty maintaining accuracy under equipment pace and time pressure, a tendency to skip first article inspection, or inability to follow protective and equipment safety requirements.

Trial activity: use an entirely fictional part drawing and tolerance requirements to practice process and operation design, clamping and alignment, measuring tool selection, and first article inspection. Ask another person to review the records.

RIASEC interest codes: RCI, Realistic–Conventional–Investigative, for machinists, and RC, Realistic–Conventional, for tool and die makers. These indicate preferences for hands-on machine operation, precise machining and assembly under procedures, and analysis of process problems. The labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

This round obtained no personality validity studies for the combined category or either suboccupation. Observe verification behavior using fictional dimensions and tooling trial records; do not use scales to decide machining authorization or release.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and may be used only for self-reflection.

Entry paths and stages of capability

BLS states that machinists typically need high school education, while tool and die makers may need postsecondary courses; common paths include on-the-job training, apprenticeships, and vocational schools. O*NET education data survey requirements for new entrants: 36% high school / 33% postsecondary certificate / 17% some college for machinists, and 41% certificate / 40% high school / 10% below high school for tool and die makers. These do not describe the education of current workers. The duration under JobZone3 describes a group.

The skill certifications described by BLS are optional evidence of capability and do not confer equipment operating permission. In China, verify skills and permits against actual tasks, machine models, and applicable rules. This round did not establish complete matches for the two occupations and does not infer the absence of a unified qualification.

Training certificates, occupational qualifications, and special operation permits, such as those for welding or lifting where applicable, are different statuses. Certification does not automatically confer equipment operating or special operation qualifications; obtain the relevant authorization under employer and regulatory requirements.

Entry stage: practice drawing interpretation, use of measuring tools, simple part machining, and first article inspection records under supervision. Learn process and safety procedures and keep process records.

Evidence to show: provide a reviewable explanation of process and inspection records, including operations, clamping, measuring tools, and first article decisions, to demonstrate the ability to machine to tolerance and record results truthfully.

Next step: check the target employer's process requirements, equipment and safety procedures, inspection standards, and authorization scope, and validate accuracy and inspection skills through supervised real machining.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may handle complex parts and CNC programming, assemble and repair dies, mentor new workers and contribute to process improvements, or move into quality inspection and production management.
Market signals and transition directions

The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook reports about 344,900 jobs in this combined category in 2025, a projected decline of about 1% during 2025–2035, a change of about -2,200, and about 30,400 annual openings, all from replacement needs. These are occupational statistics, not individual hiring probabilities, and differ from recruitment samples.

Both suboccupations involved manufacturing in 2025. BLS lists their employer shares separately and does not provide a single combined share for this page. Industry settings do not establish causes of demand or pay.

Transferable capabilities: understanding drawings and processes, dimensional measurement and inspection, machine setup and operation, CNC programming, assembly and finishing, analysis of accuracy problems, and equipment maintenance.

Moving into tool and die making requires additional training and authorization in die structures, tooling fits, assembly and finishing, trials, and fitting adjustments. General part machining does not automatically cover tooling manufacture.

items.answer: In the US, machinists typically need a high school diploma to enter, while tool and die makers may also need postsecondary courses. The occupations fall within Job Zone 3 and commonly involve long-term on-the-job training. Certification and training do not confer equipment operating or special operation qualifications. This page does not assess individual eligibility.

risks.consequence: May cause machinery and cutting tool injuries.
risks.mitigation: Operate according to procedures and wear protection.
risks.scenario: When machine tools are operated contrary to procedures or protective equipment is not worn.

risks.consequence: May cause dimensions outside tolerance and scrapped parts.
risks.mitigation: Check datums and inspect the first article before machining.
risks.scenario: When machining begins without checking datums and parameters.

risks.consequence: May cause deviations and safety hazards.
risks.mitigation: Clamp against datums and check secure fastening.
risks.scenario: When clamping or alignment is insecure.

risks.consequence: May cause machining errors across an entire batch.
risks.mitigation: Review drawings and confirm with process personnel.
risks.scenario: When drawings or specifications are misunderstood.

risks.mitigation: Follow protection and work permit requirements.
risks.scenario: When protection is absent in noisy or hazardous equipment environments.

risks.consequence: May cause entire batches of scrap and safety problems.
risks.mitigation: Stop the relevant hazardous work and report under the machine's approved abnormal condition procedures. Refer repair and blockage clearing to personnel authorized for the target task to check energy control. Do not treat a stop button as isolation or bypass guarding.
risks.scenario: When machining continues despite tool wear or abnormal equipment conditions.
risks.title: Handling abnormal equipment or tool conditions without stopping

source_card.note: This page uses the combined BLS category for two occupations: the currently verified 2025 median of 59620, hourly pay of 28.66, employment of 344900→342700 in 2035, a 2025–2035 change of -1%, and 30400 annual replacement openings are retained. Separate medians for machinists / tool and die makers are 58750/64050. Both occupations' percentiles are public, but combined percentiles were not obtained this round and are not mixed. Four 2025 suboccupation × industry pay examples are machinists in transportation equipment at 61920 / machinery at 59590, and tool and die makers in transportation equipment at 78200 / machinery at 62780. Interest codes are RCI/RC respectively. Education requirements for new entrants must be checked separately, and JobZone does not specify a fixed training period. NBS manufacturing is only a proxy; OSHA1910.147 covers only applicable US servicing work. The original shared sources and protected FAQ still contain older suboccupation projections and statements on industries, percentiles, and qualifications awaiting independent review. Gaps remain in Chinese pay and entry requirements, AI and personality evidence, and detailed industry pay for the combined category.

description.text: On this page, machinists and tool and die makers refers to the combined BLS OOH category: setting up and operating lathes, milling machines, grinding machines, and CNC equipment, machining precision metal parts, designing, assembling, and repairing tools and dies, calculating tolerances from drawings, measuring and inspecting, conducting trial runs, and making adjustments. To assess this career path, verify the work cycle, accuracy and safety boundaries, evidence scope, risk controls, and observable beginner work samples together.

title.text: Assessing Machinists and Tool and Die Makers: Work, Entry Paths, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Machinists and Tool and Die Makers
subject.summary: This page covers the combined BLS OOH category of machinists and tool and die makers, including O*NET 51-4041.00 and 51-4111.00: setting up and operating machine tools and equipment, producing precision metal parts, instruments, tools, and dies, calculating tolerances from drawings and specifications, assembling, and inspecting.
